content: Worldwide, caesarean section is the most frequently performed major surgical procedure on women. However, it is associated with several short-term complications, including hemorrhage, postoperative fever, and endometritis. The method used to deliver the placenta during a caesarean section is one factor that may influence the likelihood of these complications. Two commonly employed techniques for placental delivery during caesarean section are cord traction and manual removal. The objective of this study was to compare the outcomes of manual removal of the placenta with those of cord traction during caesarean section. A systematic search was conducted in the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register up to September 30, 2007. The analysis included all randomized controlled trials that compared manual removal with cord traction or spontaneous delivery of the placenta. Two independent reviewers assessed the studies and extracted the relevant data. A total of 15 studies involving 4,694 women were included in the analysis. Significant variability was observed in outcomes such as the duration of surgery, blood loss, and hematological parameters. Notably, two trials demonstrated that combining cord traction with uterine massage provided greater protection against blood loss. A random-effects meta-analysis was employed to evaluate these outcomes. Manual removal of the placenta was associated with a higher risk of endometritis, with a relative risk (RR) of 1.64 (95% confidence interval [CI] 1.42 to 1.90) based on data from 13 trials involving 4,134 women. It was also linked to greater blood loss, with a weighted mean difference (WMD) of 94.42 mL (95% CI 17.19 to 171.64) in eight trials involving 2,001 women. Additionally, the risk of blood loss exceeding 1,000 mL was higher with manual removal (RR 1.81, 95% CI 1.44 to 2.28) in two trials involving 872 women. Postoperative hematocrit levels were lower in women who underwent manual removal, with a WMD of -1.55% (95% CI -3.09 to -0.01) in two trials involving 384 women. Furthermore, the fall in hematocrit levels after delivery was greater with manual removal, with a WMD of 0.39% (95% CI 0.00 to 0.78) in five trials involving 1,777 women. Women who underwent manual removal also experienced a longer hospital stay, with a WMD of 0.39 days (95% CI 0.17 to 0.61) in three trials involving 546 women. The duration of surgery was shorter in one trial favoring manual removal, but this finding was not consistent across all studies. No significant differences were observed between the two methods in terms of feto-maternal hemorrhage, blood transfusion, or puerperal fever, although the number of participants studied for these outcomes was relatively small. In conclusion, delivering the placenta using cord traction during caesarean section offers several advantages over manual removal. These include a lower risk of endometritis, reduced blood loss, smaller decreases in postoperative hematocrit levels, and shorter hospital stays. Future research should focus on additional factors such as the time interval between delivery of the infant and the placenta, changes in lochia, blood splashing during placental removal, uterine pain after surgery, and the effects of delayed cord clamping.
